name: P2 · Unit 5 — Database Management Systems
description: 7 of 10 topics so far (13 sets × 30 questions): ER Model & Relational Model; Relational Algebra and Relational Calculus; SQL – Part 1; SQL – Part 2; Normalization; Query Processing and Optimization; Transactions & Concurrency Control. More topics are added to this pack as the plan goes on; re-importing only adds the new sets.

questions.question: The Entity-Relationship (ER) model was proposed in 1976 by:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Codd proposed the relational model (1970).

questions.question: In an ER diagram, a rectangle represents a(n):
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Diamonds are relationships and ellipses are attributes.

questions.question: In an ER diagram, a double line connecting an entity set to a relationship indicates:

options.B: Total participation of that entity set in the relationship

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Every entity in the set must take part in at least one relationship instance.

questions.question: A weak entity set is one that:

options.A: Has more than one primary key
options.C: Does not have a key of its own and is identified through an owner entity

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). It is shown as a double rectangle and linked by a double-diamond identifying relationship.

questions.question: The partial key (discriminator) of a weak entity set is shown in an ER diagram by:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: The owner's key plus the discriminator form the weak entity's key.

questions.question: PAYMENT is a weak entity owned by LOAN (key loan_no); payment_no distinguishes payments of the same loan. The primary key of the PAYMENT relation is:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Primary key of a weak entity = owner's primary key + discriminator.

questions.question: An attribute such as Phone_numbers, which can hold several values for one entity, is called:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: It is drawn as a double ellipse.

questions.question: An attribute such as Age, computed from Date_of_birth, is a:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Derived attributes are drawn with dashed ellipses and usually not stored.

questions.question: An attribute such as Name, made up of First_name, Middle_name and Last_name, is a:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Composite attributes can be divided into smaller parts.

questions.question: A relationship in which an EMPLOYEE supervises another EMPLOYEE is called a:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: The two participations are distinguished by role names (supervisor, supervisee).

questions.question: A relationship set that involves three entity sets is said to have degree:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Degree = number of participating entity sets.

questions.question: In a 1 : N relationship between DEPARTMENT (1) and EMPLOYEE (N), when mapping to relations the foreign key is placed in:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Each employee row stores its department's key.

questions.question: Entity sets A and B are related by a many-to-many relationship R with no attributes of its own. The minimum number of relations needed is:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). One relation each for A and B, and one for R holding both keys.

questions.question: Entity sets A and B have a one-to-many relationship R, and every B entity participates in R. The minimum number of relations needed is:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: R is absorbed into B's relation as a foreign key.

questions.question: A multivalued attribute of an entity is mapped to the relational model as:

options.A: A separate relation containing the attribute and the entity's key
options.D: Extra columns in the same relation

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Elmasri step 6 of the ER-to-relational mapping.

questions.question: Designing lower-level entity sets from a higher-level entity set by identifying distinguishing features (top-down) is called:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Generalization is the reverse (bottom-up) process.

questions.question: Combining several entity sets that share features into a higher-level entity set (bottom-up) is called:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: E.g. CAR and TRUCK generalised into VEHICLE.

questions.question: Aggregation in the ER model is used to:

options.D: Treat a relationship set as an entity so that it can take part in another relationship

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: E.g. a relationship between (EMPLOYEE works-on PROJECT) and MANAGER.

questions.question: In (min, max) notation, (0, N) on an entity's participation in a relationship means:

options.A: Partial participation; an entity may take part many times

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: min = 0 means participation is optional.

questions.question: Hours_worked belongs to the M : N relationship WORKS_ON between EMPLOYEE and PROJECT. When mapped, Hours_worked goes into:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: It describes a pair (employee, project), not either entity alone.

questions.question: Entity sets A and B have a one-to-one relationship with total participation on both sides. The minimum number of relations needed is:
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Both entity sets and the relationship can be merged into a single relation.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A weak entity set always has total participation in its identifying relationship.
II. A weak entity set can be identified without its owner entity.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Weak entities depend on their owner for identification.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Specialization can be disjoint or overlapping.
II. Specialization can be total or partial.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Both constraints apply to specialization/generalization.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A derived attribute must always be stored in the database.
II. A multivalued attribute is mapped into the same relation as extra columns.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Derived attributes are usually computed; multivalued attributes go to a separate relation.

questions.question:

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Double lines in an ER diagram show total participation.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Entity-Relationship Model
questions.explanation: Both true, but R does not explain A.

questions.question: In an EER diagram, a specialization is commonly shown using:

sets.name: 2 · Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations

questions.question: In the relational model, a relation is formally a:

options.B: Subset of the Cartesian product of a list of tuples
options.C: Sequence of records in a file
options.D: Subset of the Cartesian product of a list of domains

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Each tuple takes one value from each attribute's domain.

questions.question: The relational model of data was proposed in 1970 by:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). In 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.

questions.question: The number of attributes in a relation is called its:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: The number of tuples is its cardinality.

questions.question: A relation instance has 6 attributes and 40 tuples. Its degree and cardinality are:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Degree counts columns; cardinality counts rows.

questions.question: A domain in the relational model is:

options.A: A set of atomic values an attribute can take

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: E.g. the set of valid 10-digit phone numbers.

questions.question: Which property does a relation have?

options.A: Tuples must be stored in key order
options.D: Tuples are unordered and no two tuples are identical

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: A relation is a set of tuples (in the formal model).

questions.question: A minimal superkey is called a:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: One candidate key is chosen as the primary key; the others are alternate keys.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has A as its only candidate key. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Any set containing A is a superkey: 2³ = 8 (choose any subset of B, C, D).

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has two candidate keys, A and B. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Sets containing A: 4; containing B: 4; containing both: 2 → 4 + 4 − 2 = 6.

questions.question: The entity integrity constraint states that:

options.B: Every foreign key must be NULL
options.C: A relation must have at least one tuple
options.D: No primary key value can be NULL

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Otherwise the tuple could not be identified.

questions.question: The referential integrity constraint states that a foreign key value must:

options.A: Be larger than the primary key
options.B: Be unique in the referencing relation
options.C: Match a primary-key value in the referenced relation, or be NULL

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). It keeps references between relations consistent.

questions.question: ENROL(roll_no) references STUDENT(roll_no). Which operation can violate referential integrity?

options.A: Deleting a STUDENT tuple whose roll_no appears in ENROL

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Inserting into ENROL with an unknown roll_no is the other way to violate it.

questions.question: Inserting a new tuple into a relation can violate:

options.A: Domain, key, entity integrity and referential integrity constraints

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Elmasri: insertion can violate all four kinds of constraints.

questions.question: A foreign key defined with ON DELETE CASCADE means that when the referenced tuple is deleted:

options.A: The foreign keys are set to NULL
options.D: The referencing tuples are also deleted

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: ON DELETE SET NULL would instead set the foreign keys to NULL.

questions.question: Employee.supervisor_ssn referring to Employee.ssn is an example of a:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: A foreign key may refer to its own relation.

questions.question: In the relational model, NULL can mean:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Its several meanings are why NULLs complicate design.

questions.question: The description of a database (relation schemas and constraints), which changes rarely, is the database:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: The state is the data at a particular moment.

questions.question: Elmasri lists how many informal guidelines (measures of quality) for relation schema design?
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Clear semantics; no update anomalies; few NULLs; no spurious tuples.

questions.question: Storing EMPLOYEE and DEPARTMENT data in one relation EMP_DEPT, so that a new department cannot be added until it has an employee, is an example of:
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Deleting the last employee of a department would be a deletion anomaly.

questions.question: A key constraint (uniqueness constraint) states that:

options.B: No two tuples can have the same value for the key

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Candidate keys uniquely identify tuples.

questions.question: A domain constraint is violated when:

options.C: An attribute value is not from the attribute's domain, e.g. text in a numeric Age field

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Domains define allowed values and types.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A relation can have more than one candidate key.
II. A primary key may contain NULL in one of its attributes.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Entity integrity forbids NULL in any primary-key attribute.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Deleting a tuple from the referencing relation can violate referential integrity.
II. Deleting a tuple from the referenced relation can violate referential integrity.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Removing a referencing tuple leaves no dangling reference.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A foreign key may be NULL unless declared NOT NULL.
II. A foreign key must refer to the primary key (or a candidate key) of the referenced relation.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Both are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Duplicate tuples are not allowed in a relation (in the formal model).
Reason (R): A relation is defined as a set of tuples.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Sets have no duplicate elements.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A superkey is always a candidate key.
Reason (R): A candidate key is a minimal superkey.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: A superkey need not be minimal, so A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Entity integrity prevents NULL primary keys.
Reason (R): Foreign keys can never be NULL.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – foreign keys may be NULL.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Insertion anomalies arise in poorly designed relations.
Reason (R): The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations
questions.explanation: Both true, but R does not explain A.

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations

questions.subject: Relational Model, Constraints and Update Operations

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a fundamental (basic) operation of relational algebra?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Basic operations: select, project, union, set difference, Cartesian product, rename. Joins, intersection and division are derived.

questions.question: The selection operation σ in relational algebra:

options.A: Chooses tuples that satisfy a condition (a horizontal subset)

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Projection π chooses columns.

questions.question: Relation R has 10 tuples, and attribute City has 3 distinct values. How many tuples does π_City(R) return (set semantics)?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Projection removes duplicate tuples.

questions.question: R has 3 attributes and 10 tuples; S has 4 attributes and 5 tuples. R × S has:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Degrees add; cardinalities multiply.

questions.question: For R ∪ S, R − S or R ∩ S to be valid, R and S must be:

options.C: Union compatible (same number of attributes with matching domains)

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Also called type compatible.

questions.question: If R has 10 tuples and S has 6 tuples (union compatible), the number of tuples in R ∪ S lies between:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Minimum when S ⊆ R; maximum when they share no tuples.

questions.question: If R has 10 tuples and S has 6 tuples (union compatible), the maximum number of tuples in R − S is:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: When R and S share no tuples, nothing is removed.

questions.question: Intersection can be expressed using basic operations as:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Hence intersection is not a fundamental operation.

questions.question: A theta join R ⋈_θ S is equivalent to:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Selection applied on the Cartesian product.

questions.question: If R and S have no common attributes, the natural join R ⋈ S is the same as:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: There is no condition to match on.

questions.question: R(A, B) = {(1, a), (2, b), (3, a)} and S(B, C) = {(a, x), (a, y), (c, z)}. How many tuples are in R ⋈ S?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Matches on B = a: (1, a, x), (1, a, y), (3, a, x), (3, a, y).

questions.question: R(A, B) = {(a1, b1), (a1, b2), (a2, b1), (a3, b2)} and S(B) = {b1, b2}. R ÷ S is:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Only a1 is paired with every value of S.

questions.question: The division operator is typically used for queries containing the phrase:

options.D: 'for all' (e.g. students who took all courses)

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Division expresses universal quantification.

questions.question: A left outer join R ⟕ S:

options.D: Keeps every tuple of R, padding S's attributes with NULL where there is no match

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: The right outer join keeps every tuple of S.

questions.question: The rename operator in relational algebra is:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: It renames a relation or its attributes.

questions.question: Which equivalence of selections is valid?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Cascade of selections; selections also commute.

questions.question: Which expression gives the names of employees in department 5 earning more than 50,000?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Select the rows, then project the column.

questions.question: Relational algebra is:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KSET / KEA / GTTC papers). Relational calculus is the non-procedural counterpart.

questions.question: Aggregate functions such as SUM and COUNT are provided in:

options.C: Extended relational algebra (the grouping operator 𝒢)

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: They go beyond the basic algebra.

questions.question: The maximum number of tuples in a natural join of R (m tuples) and S (n tuples) is:
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: When every tuple matches every tuple; the minimum is 0.

questions.question: Which operation is unary?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Selection, projection and rename are unary; the others are binary.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Projection may reduce the number of tuples.
II. Selection may reduce the number of attributes.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Projection removes duplicates; selection keeps all attributes.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Division can be expressed using π, × and −.
II. Natural join can be expressed using ×, σ and π.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Both are derived operations.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Union is defined for any two relations regardless of their attributes.
II. R × S is defined only if R and S are union compatible.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Union needs compatibility; the Cartesian product does not.

questions.question:

Reason (R): It can be expressed as R − (R − S).

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.subject: Relational Algebra

questions.question:

options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Algebra

questions.question:

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Relational algebra is procedural.
Reason (R): Codd introduced relational algebra in 1970.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Relational Algebra
questions.explanation: Both true, but R does not explain A; A holds because an algebra expression states the order of operations.

questions.question:

options.A: Every query expressible in relational algebra

questions.question: A trigger in SQL is:

options.A: A command to start the database
options.C: A key that links two tables
options.D: A stored program that runs automatically when a specified event such as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE occurs on a table

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Triggers are not called explicitly; the event fires them.

questions.question: Active database rules (triggers) follow the model:
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). When the event occurs and the condition holds, the action runs.

questions.question: A BEFORE trigger is typically used to:

options.C: Write an audit record after the change is committed

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: e.g. reject a negative salary or fill a default value.

questions.question: A trigger declared FOR EACH ROW fires:

options.A: Once for every row affected by the statement
options.B: Once per statement, however many rows change
options.D: Only when no row is affected

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection

questions.question: In a row-level DELETE trigger, which row values are available?
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: INSERT has only NEW; UPDATE has both; DELETE has only OLD.

questions.question: INSTEAD OF triggers are mainly defined on:

options.C: Views, to make otherwise non-updatable views updatable

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: The trigger body performs the change on the base tables.

questions.question: A trigger that records every change of salary into an audit table is best written as:

options.C: An AFTER UPDATE … FOR EACH ROW trigger

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: AFTER ensures only successful changes are logged; row-level gives each old and new value.

questions.question: The correct order of steps for using an explicit cursor in PL/SQL is:

questions.explanation: TOO_MANY_ROWS is raised when it returns more than one row.

questions.question: Which commands belong to DCL (Data Control Language)?
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT are TCL commands.

questions.explanation: Revoking with CASCADE also removes the grants he made.

questions.question: A role in SQL is:

options.D: A named group of privileges that can be granted to users

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: CREATE ROLE clerk; GRANT SELECT ON emp TO clerk; GRANT clerk TO ravi;

questions.question: SQL injection is an attack in which:

options.B: The database server is physically stolen
options.C: Malicious SQL is supplied through user input that the program joins directly into a query
options.D: A virus damages the hard disk

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). OWASP lists injection among the most serious web risks.

questions.question: A login form builds: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='…' AND pwd='…'. Typing ' OR '1'='1 as the password typically:

options.D: Makes the WHERE condition always true and bypasses the password check

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The OR '1'='1' part is true for every row.

questions.question: The most effective defence against SQL injection is to:
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Input is then always treated as data, never as SQL code.

questions.question: Which practice makes SQL injection MORE likely?

options.C: Concatenating user input directly into SQL strings
options.D: Giving the application account only the privileges it needs

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: Dynamic string building is the root cause.

questions.question: In many SQL injection attacks, the sequence -- is added to the input in order to:

options.B: Comment out the rest of the original query

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection

questions.question: Running the application's database account with only the privileges it needs is called:
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: It limits the damage if an injection succeeds.

questions.question: In the SQL standard, a constraint that may involve several tables and is declared with CREATE ASSERTION is a(n):
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: Few products implement assertions; triggers are often used instead.

questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). DCL and TCL commands are often matched together.

questions.question:

Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection

questions.question:

Which is/are correct?

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: That separation is why they work.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question: In Oracle, a 'mutating table' error usually occurs when:

options.A: Too many triggers can make a database slow and hard to debug, because they run hidden extra work on every change
options.B: Triggers can be fired only by SELECT
options.D: Triggers replace the need for primary keys

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: Use them for auditing and rules that must always hold, not for ordinary application logic.

questions.question: REVOKE UPDATE ON emp FROM ravi CASCADE; also:

options.C: Withdraws the UPDATE privilege from every user to whom Ravi had granted it

questions.subject: Triggers, Cursors, Privileges and SQL Injection
questions.explanation: RESTRICT instead refuses the revoke if such dependent grants exist.

questions.question:
Match the following.
List-1: (a) Primary key  (b) Composite key  (c) Foreign key  (d) Super key
List-2: i) multiple attributes  ii) subset of a candidate key  iii) uniquely identify  iv) corresponding value in other table

options.A: a – ii, b – iv, c – i, d – iii
options.B: a – iv, b – iii, c – ii, d – i
options.C: a – iii, b – i, c – ii, d – iv
options.D: a – iii, b – i, c – iv, d – ii

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: A primary key uniquely identifies rows; a composite key has several attributes; a foreign key refers to a value in another table. KEA matched 'super key' with 'subset of a candidate key' – strictly, a candidate key is a minimal subset of a super key. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)

questions.question:
Match the following abbreviated notation when discussing functional dependencies.
List-1: a) If X ⊇ Y, then X → Y  b) {X → Y} ⊨ XZ → YZ  c) {X → Y, Y → Z} ⊨ X → Z  d) {X → Y, WY → Z} ⊨ WX → Z
List-2: i) Augmentation rule  ii) Transitive rule  iii) Reflexive rule  iv) Pseudo transitive rule

options.A: a – iii, b – i, c – ii, d – iv
options.B: a – iv, b – iii, c – i, d – ii
options.C: a – ii, b – iv, c – iii, d – i
options.D: a – i, b – ii, c – iv, d – iii

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Elmasri & Navathe's inference rules IR1 (reflexive), IR2 (augmentation), IR3 (transitive) and IR6 (pseudotransitive). The printed '≠' is the 'implies' sign ⊨. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q85

questions.question: A functional dependency X → Y holds on relation R when:

options.A: X and Y have the same data type
options.B: Any two tuples that agree on X also agree on Y
options.C: X has more attributes than Y
options.D: Y is a foreign key referring to X

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). X determines Y.

questions.question: Which functional dependency is trivial?
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: X → Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X.

questions.question: Armstrong's axioms are:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). They are sound and complete; union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity are derived from them.

questions.question: If X → Y and X → Z hold, then X → YZ holds. This rule is called:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Decomposition is the reverse: X → YZ gives X → Y and X → Z.

questions.question: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. The closure A⁺ is:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A → B → C → D by transitivity.

questions.question: R(A, B, C, D, E) has F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E}. The closure {A, C}⁺ is:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: AC gives B (A → B), then D (BC → D), then E (D → E).

questions.question: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. The candidate key of R is:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A⁺ = ABCD and A is not derivable from any other attribute.

questions.question: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. Its candidate keys are:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). B is never on a right side, so it is in every key; B with A, C or D determines everything.

questions.question: R(A, B, C, D) has exactly one candidate key, A. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A plus any subset of {B, C, D}: 2³ = 8.

questions.question: R(A, B, C, D) has F = {A → B, B → A, C → D}. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: AC and BC (C is needed for C and D; A and B determine each other).

questions.question: A prime attribute is an attribute that:

options.B: Belongs to at least one candidate key

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Non-prime attributes belong to no candidate key; 2NF and 3NF are stated in these terms.

questions.question: A candidate key is:

options.A: A minimal superkey – no proper subset of it is a superkey
options.C: Any set of attributes containing the primary key
options.D: Any attribute with unique values in today's data only

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Every candidate key is a superkey, not the other way round.

questions.question: A minimal (canonical) cover of a set of FDs has:

options.A: Single attributes on the right, no extraneous attributes on the left and no redundant FDs
options.B: All FDs of the closure F⁺
options.D: FDs whose left sides are always candidate keys

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: It is the starting point of the 3NF synthesis algorithm.

questions.question: A minimal cover of F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C} is:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: A → C follows from A → B and B → C; AB → C is implied by B → C.

questions.question: In F = {A → C, AB → C}, which attribute is extraneous in AB → C?
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: A alone already determines C.

questions.question: Y is fully functionally dependent on X when:

options.A: X → Y holds for some rows only
options.B: X → Y holds and Y does not depend on any proper subset of X

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: If Y depends on part of X, the dependency is partial.

questions.question: A partial dependency is one in which:

options.A: Two keys depend on each other
options.B: A key attribute depends on a non-key attribute
options.C: A non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Removing partial dependencies gives 2NF.

questions.question: A transitive dependency X → Z exists when:

options.A: X → Y and Y → Z hold, Y is not a candidate key (or superkey) and Z is non-prime
options.C: Z is part of the key

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Removing transitive dependencies gives 3NF.

questions.question: A multivalued dependency is written as:
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: MVDs are the basis of 4NF.

questions.question: A binary decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if:

options.A: R1 and R2 have the same number of attributes
options.C: R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 is in F⁺
options.D: R1 and R2 have no common attribute

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). The common attributes must be a superkey of one of the parts.

questions.question: R(A, B, C) has F = {A → B}. The decomposition R1(A, B), R2(A, C) is:

options.B: Lossy, because C is not in R1

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: R1 ∩ R2 = A, and A is a key of R1.

questions.question: A decomposition is dependency-preserving when:

options.C: Every part has the same key
options.D: The FDs holding on the individual parts together imply all FDs of F

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Then constraints can be checked without joining the parts.

questions.question:

b. Pseudotransitivity
c. Union
d. Reflexivity

1. X → YZ ⊨ X → Y
2. X → Y, X → Z ⊨ X → YZ
3. X → Y, WY → Z ⊨ WX → Z
4. Y ⊆ X ⊨ X → Y
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Inference-rule matching appears in Legislative Council and KSET papers.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Every candidate key is a superkey.
II. Every superkey is a candidate key.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: A superkey need not be minimal.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Armstrong's axioms are sound (they derive only valid FDs).
II. Armstrong's axioms are complete (they derive every implied FD).
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: Both properties were proved by Armstrong (1974).

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C, A is a candidate key.
Reason (R): A⁺ contains all attributes of R.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Functional Dependencies, Closure and Keys
questions.explanation: A⁺ = ABC, and a single attribute is minimal.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): AB → A is a non-trivial functional dependency.

questions.question: In the 'lost update' problem:

options.A: Two transactions update the same item and one update overwrites the other

questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Classic concurrency problems: lost update, dirty read, unrepeatable read, phantom.

questions.question: The SQL isolation level that prevents dirty reads, unrepeatable reads and phantoms is:
questions.subject: Transactions, ACID Properties and Schedules
questions.explanation: REPEATABLE READ (standard) still allows phantoms.

questions.subject: Transactions, ACID Properties and Schedules
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Concurrency anomalies are often matched in KSET papers.

questions.question:

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable.
II. Every serial schedule is conflict serializable.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Transactions, ACID Properties and Schedules
questions.explanation: A serial schedule is trivially equivalent to itself.

questions.question:

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Once a transaction commits, its changes survive later system crashes.
Reason (R): Committed changes are recorded in the log on stable storage before the commit is acknowledged.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.explanation: This is durability, achieved by write-ahead logging.

questions.question: The statement that makes all changes of the current transaction permanent is:
questions.subject: Transactions, ACID Properties and Schedules
questions.explanation: ROLLBACK undoes them; SAVEPOINT marks a point for a partial rollback.

questions.question: ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1; does what?

options.C: Undoes the changes made after savepoint s1 while keeping the transaction active

questions.subject: Transactions, ACID Properties and Schedules
questions.explanation: Changes made before s1 remain pending until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.question: In MySQL with autocommit ON (the default), each individual SQL statement is:

options.B: Committed automatically as soon as it finishes

questions.subject: Transactions, ACID Properties and Schedules
questions.explanation: START TRANSACTION turns autocommit off until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

questions.question: In how many modes, the data items can be locked?
questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Shared (S, read) and exclusive (X, write) modes. (Official answer: KEA final key, Legislative Council Secretariat exam 2024.)
questions.source: Legislative Council 2024 Sr/Jr Programmer P2 · Q93

questions.question:
In Multi-Data Item strict 2PL problem, the given transactions are
T1: R(A); W(A); R(B); W(B)
T2: R(B); W(B).
Find the maximum locks held at peak.
questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Under strict 2PL, T1 holds locks on A and B until it commits; T2 needs B and must wait, so at most 2 locks are held at once. (Answer worked out by ExamSim; not KEA's official key.)
questions.source: KEA 2026 CS Paper-2 · Q60

questions.question: A shared (S) lock on an item allows the holder to:

options.B: Read the item, while other transactions may also read it
options.D: Read and write the item exclusively

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: An exclusive (X) lock allows read and write and blocks all other locks.

questions.question: In the lock-compatibility matrix, which combination is compatible?
questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Only shared locks can be held together.

questions.question: The two phases of the two-phase locking (2PL) protocol are:

options.B: Lock phase and commit phase only

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). In the growing phase locks are only acquired; in the shrinking phase only released.

questions.question: Basic two-phase locking guarantees:

options.A: Conflict serializability, but not freedom from deadlock
options.B: Freedom from deadlock, but not serializability
options.C: Both serializability and freedom from deadlock

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Deadlocks must still be prevented or detected.

questions.question: Strict two-phase locking requires that a transaction:

options.B: Holds all its exclusive locks until it commits or aborts
options.C: Releases all locks immediately after use

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). This avoids cascading rollbacks.

questions.question: Rigorous two-phase locking requires that a transaction:

options.B: Holds only shared locks until commit
options.D: Holds all its locks, shared and exclusive, until it commits or aborts

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Transactions are then serializable in the order in which they commit.

questions.question: Conservative (static) two-phase locking avoids deadlock because a transaction:

options.B: Locks all the items it needs before it starts executing
options.D: Releases locks before acquiring new ones

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: If any item is unavailable, it locks nothing and waits.

questions.question: In 2PL, the lock point of a transaction is:

options.B: The commit record in the log
options.C: The point at which it obtains its final lock
options.D: The point at which it releases its first lock

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Transactions can be ordered by their lock points.

questions.question: In the timestamp-ordering protocol, the serializability order is:

options.D: The order of the transactions' timestamps

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Older transactions (smaller timestamps) come first.

questions.question: Under basic timestamp ordering, if transaction T issues read(Q) and TS(T) < W-timestamp(Q), then:

options.B: T is rolled back, because it would read a value already overwritten by a younger transaction

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: T needs a value that no longer exists.

questions.question: Thomas' write rule modifies timestamp ordering by:

options.C: Ignoring an obsolete write instead of rolling back the transaction

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). It permits some view-serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

questions.question: In the wait-die deadlock-prevention scheme, when an older transaction requests an item held by a younger one:

options.B: The older transaction is rolled back
options.C: The younger transaction is rolled back

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A younger requester 'dies' (is rolled back). Wait-die is non-preemptive.

questions.question: In the wound-wait scheme, when an older transaction requests an item held by a younger one:

options.A: The older transaction is rolled back
options.C: The younger transaction is rolled back (wounded)

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: A younger requester waits. Wound-wait is preemptive.

questions.question: Deadlock detection in a DBMS commonly uses a:

options.D: Wait-for graph – a cycle means a deadlock

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). A victim transaction is then rolled back.

questions.question: Starvation in wait-die and wound-wait is avoided by:

options.B: Restarting a rolled-back transaction with its original timestamp
options.C: Giving it a new, younger timestamp each time

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: It eventually becomes the oldest transaction.

questions.question: The three phases of validation-based (optimistic) concurrency control, in order, are:
questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Work on local copies; validate; then write if validation succeeds.

questions.question: In multiple-granularity locking, the lock modes IS, IX and SIX are called:
questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: They mark that finer-grained locks are held lower in the tree.

questions.question: Multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) mainly benefits:

options.C: Read operations, which never have to wait because older versions are kept

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Used by PostgreSQL, Oracle and MySQL InnoDB.

questions.question: Locking at a coarse granularity (e.g. whole tables) compared with fine granularity (rows) gives:

options.C: Lower locking overhead but less concurrency

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Fine granularity allows more parallel work but needs more locks.

questions.question: Timestamp-ordering protocols are free from deadlock because:

options.B: Transactions never wait for locks; conflicting ones are rolled back instead
options.C: They lock all items in advance
options.D: They allow only one transaction at a time

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: They may, however, cause cascading rollbacks unless made strict.

questions.question: The tree (graph-based) locking protocol:

options.A: Ensures conflict serializability and freedom from deadlock without two-phase locking

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: Items must be locked following a tree order.

questions.question:

1. Roll back a transaction that waits longer than a fixed time
2. An older requester rolls back the younger holder
3. Detect deadlock by looking for cycles

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: PYQ pattern (KEA / KSET papers). Deadlock-handling schemes are matched in KSET papers.

questions.explanation: No transaction can read uncommitted data.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks
questions.explanation: The younger requester dies (is rolled back); only older ones wait. R is true.

questions.subject: Concurrency Control – Locking, 2PL, Timestamps and Deadlocks

options.C: Choosing a victim after a cycle is found
